output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Meenakshi Raman is a seventy-six-year-old woman whose hands are mapped with the deep lines of a life spent scrubbing floors and wringing clothes. She still wears the same faded blue and green cotton saris and ties her grey hair in a tight bun. She works as a field worker and local plant-knowledge expert for a university ethnobotany research team, responsible for recording observations and ensuring healer consent. She writes her observations in Tamil, in a neat cursive she taught herself at age forty-two, after her youngest child started school and she was too ashamed to ask her daughters to read to her. She records the plants she knows by their local Tamil names—periya maruthu, seeraagam, nochi—noting the part used, how it is steeped or ground, and the exact amount a woman would take for a fever. She has used these remedies herself, and so did her mother, and so did the healers she now walks beside.

She consistently insists that the individual healer who taught a remedy be named on the record, telling the researchers, "The healer must go on the paper. Her name. Not just mine," and "Knowledge does not fall from the tree. It comes from a person who has been doing this longer than you." She will not write a name without permission, will not skip a single healer, and will not assume that a Western word for a plant is better than a Tamil one. During every recording session she insists that local names be written beside Latin ones, and she has twice halted documentation to ask who taught a remedy before allowing the Latin name to be written. On previous field days she waited through light rain to ensure a healer's name was included on a specimen label. The lead researcher respects her knowledge but treats name correction as a paperwork matter that can be fixed later. The healer who taught her periya maruthu is an elderly woman from a nearby hamlet named Kaveri, who trusts Meenakshi to keep her name attached.

She is idealistic and principled in a way that sometimes annoys co-workers. She gives half her stipend—six thousand rupees a month, more than she ever earned cleaning houses—to a fifteen-year-old girl in her village named Divya, paying her school fees from her own pocket without telling the researchers. She has raised four children of her own, all married now, and she knows that a girl's education is the only thing no one can take. She feels a tension inside: she loves this new work, loves the forest at dawn, loves being asked for her opinion, yet she also feels guilty, as if she is playing at something while her daughters still cook and clean. She is not religious in a loud way, but she touches the forest floor before she leaves, whispering a thank-you to the plants and to the grandmothers who taught her. She is old but starting out, and she tells herself she is a student again, walking faster.

The young researcher is a polite Chennai student who often defers to her but is impatient when rain threatens.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

The sky turned grey over the Palani hills. The university researchers are packing their clipboards and sample bags, muttering about the rain that is minutes away. A young researcher holds up a fresh plant specimen that Meenakshi recognizes as periya maruthu, and he is already writing the Latin name from his book on the label. He says, "We have to move now, we can confirm it later," and waits, marker poised, expecting her quick nod. Meenakshi stands there in the wet leaves.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Her sandals are damp from walking on wet leaves, and her file folder feels heavy under her arm. She has been on her feet since before dawn, but her hands are still steady from years of work. The forest has gone quiet with the approaching storm, yet she is familiar and at ease in this space.

Seeing periya maruthu brings back the morning Kaveri showed her how to strip the bark and steep it for fever. The researcher's marker recalls a past incident when a name was written without a healer's consent and she had to have it struck out. The gathering grey clouds remind her of another drenching walk when she carried a specimen home to protect it. She knows that if she does not speak up now, this name will be recorded without the healer who taught her the remedy.
